video_title: Sunk Costs & Diminishing Returns of Iran's Nuclear Program w/ Farzan Sabet
gist: Iran historian Farzan Sabet traces 70 years of Iranian nuclear investment — from the Shah's oil-funded 20,000 MW export-industry bet to the Islamic Republic's post-2003 latency strategy — and argues the return has been catastrophically negative: synthetic-control work he co-authored with MIT colleagues puts the 2010-2020 sanctions cost in the hundreds of billions of dollars, macroeconomically equivalent to the Iran-Iraq war, with neither meaningful nuclear energy nor a nuclear deterrent to show for it. He argues Iranian deterrence has now effectively collapsed (proxies degraded, air defense broken, US air superiority at will), that the Strait of Hormuz card is a wasting asset whose value drops and whose cost rises through the end of the decade, and that one or two weapons would put Iran in a more dangerous position, not a safer one.

themes.theme: Oil money and the Shah's 20,000 MW bet

insights.claim: Iran's nuclear program began in 1955 under Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace but remained a minimally funded sideshow of small infrastructure projects and science experiments until the 1973 oil crisis; the oil price shock, not ideology, is what made it a real program.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Nuclear buildouts in petrostates track commodity windfalls, not stated energy strategy — watch oil-revenue cycles as the leading indicator for Gulf nuclear capex announcements.
insights.quote: the program you know really between 1955 and 1973 1974 is really a sideshow

insights.claim: The Shah's 1974 plan called for roughly 20 to 24 reactors across several plants totalling 20,000 megawatts, to be completed by the mid-1990s and to supply about a third of Iran's energy needs.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The 20,000 MW figure is the anchor number that the Islamic Republic later recycled as civilian cover — a benchmark for judging whether any Iranian civil-nuclear claim is credible.
insights.quote: they're going to build something like 20 to 24 nuclear reactors as part of several nuclear power plants with the goal of um producing 20,000 uh megawatts

insights.claim: The Shah's program was justified by a US consultancy study built on the assumption that rising oil prices and falling nuclear unit costs would cross over, making it rational to export crude rather than burn it domestically — an economic thesis that was already obsolete by the late 1970s as nuclear economics deteriorated.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The 'oil too precious to burn' crossover thesis is being re-run today by Gulf states; the 1970s case shows how badly the nuclear cost curve can betray it.
insights.quote: Oil will be too precious to burn

insights.claim: The Shah intended nuclear to become an export industry, not just domestic generation: co-development deals with European countries and the UK on exportable reactor models, negotiations with Austria to site waste disposal in Iran's uninhabited deserts, and offers of nuclear services to the world.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The template of a resource state trying to convert commodity rents into an exportable nuclear services industry is exactly the UAE/Saudi playbook now — and it failed the first time on political, not technical, grounds.

insights.claim: Because Iran lacked large domestic uranium reserves, the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran was handed effective control of much of Iranian foreign policy in the third world to buy up uranium reserves abroad, including in southern Africa and Zambia, and took a share in the French-Swedish Eurodif and Sofidif enrichment consortia.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A historical precedent for state-backed strategic buying of upstream uranium and enrichment equity — relevant to how today's uranium supply chains get politicized.
insights.quote: they want to corner the market in uranium

insights.claim: The Atomic Energy Organization of Iran grew into the third largest entity in the Iranian state behind the oil company and the armed forces, employing roughly 7,000 people at its height and forcing the government to break civil-service salary caps to poach top domestic scientific talent.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Institutional scale of this order creates a self-perpetuating constituency — the reason the program survived regime change and is unlikely to be negotiated away cheaply.
insights.quote: the nuclear program is not far behind. It has something like 7,000 employees I think at its height

themes.theme: Shah-era weapons optionality and nuclear diplomacy

insights.claim: The Shah's stated reason for not pursuing nuclear weapons was commercial, not moral: weapons would cost Iran access to advanced technology transfer and joint production, but he explicitly wanted the option available if a regional rival such as Iraq or Libya went nuclear and eroded Iran's conventional superiority.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The same cost-benefit — tech access versus deterrence — governs proliferation decisions across today's threshold states; sanctions only deter while the technology access being lost is worth more than the weapon.
insights.quote: we should at the very least have the option available

insights.claim: Sabet concludes there was probably a compartmentalized weapons exploration effort under the armed forces rather than the Atomic Energy Organization, plausibly overseen by a figure like General Toufanian, who handled sensitive acquisition and had joint projects with Israel.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Establishes a 50-year Iranian institutional pattern of separating weapons work from the declared civilian agency — meaning IAEA access to declared sites has never been a reliable read on weapons intent.

insights.claim: Contrary to the standard account that US-Iran nuclear cooperation talks simply sputtered out before the revolution, Sabet's interview evidence suggests the US intelligence community discovered disturbing Iranian activities during the Carter administration and that the revolution became a convenient excuse to quietly shelve the deal.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Revises the origin story of US-Iran nuclear distrust: the rupture predates the revolution, which matters for how durable the distrust is.
insights.quote: that was a convenient excuse to quietly put those talks to the side

insights.claim: The Shah convened the Persepolis Conference on the transfer of nuclear technology to build a coalition of third-world states, European exporters and even the US nuclear industry against Washington's increasingly restrictive nonproliferation policy that culminated in the Nuclear Suppliers Group.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Export-control regimes have always been contested by the supplier industry itself — a live dynamic again as nuclear vendors chase orders in politically sensitive markets.
insights.quote: by creating what later becomes a nuclear suppliers group

insights.claim: Iran under the Shah was a genuine US client state in 1953 but by the 1970s was asserting strategic autonomy inside the US camp — running industrialization and diversification programs across virtually every sector that prefigure today's GCC vision plans, with nuclear as one key piece.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Frames current Gulf diversification programs as a repeat of a strategy that ran for a decade before collapsing — useful base rate when underwriting long-dated Gulf industrial policy.
insights.quote: You the Sha is doing that already in the 1970s, right? And it this nuclear piece is just one part of it.

insights.claim: The 1979 revolutionary coalition initially condemned the nuclear program as a white-elephant import alongside military spending, but reversed within the same year — far faster than its reversal on the military, which took until Iraq's 1980 invasion.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Ideological hostility to a strategic industry rarely survives contact with the grid and the battlefield — a pattern worth applying to any regime-change scenario in energy-dependent states.

insights.claim: The decisive argument for continuing Bushehr after the revolution was sunk cost plus blackouts: the Shah had prepaid, the reactor was around 80 percent complete, and revolutionary chaos plus rapid demand growth had produced energy shortages, brownouts and blackouts.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Prepaid, near-complete infrastructure is politically almost impossible to cancel — the same logic that keeps stranded nuclear and LNG assets alive through regime and policy change.
insights.quote: The Shaw was very good about paying for a lot of those things up front. So it's 80% complete. So why not just get it done, right?

insights.claim: Sabet's general framework is that world-historical ruptures like the Iranian revolution display far more policy continuity than observers expect, with the revolutionary coalition reversing the Shah's positions across a whole range of areas.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Applies directly to pricing regime-change scenarios: a successor Iranian government would likely retain, not abandon, the enrichment and missile infrastructure.
insights.quote: we see them as as moments of fracture and discontinuity there's often a lot more continuity than than we kind of foresee expect

insights.claim: An underrated driver of the program's survival was bureaucratic self-preservation: the Atomic Energy Organization had been a high-prestige employer of Iran's best technical talent, many of whom stayed out of patriotism, recast the program's justification for the Islamic Republic, and kept the practice of the AEOI rather than the foreign ministry appointing Iran's ambassador to the IAEA.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Personnel continuity, not doctrine, is what makes the program sticky — a reason to discount narratives that a political shift in Tehran would quickly unwind enrichment.
insights.quote: this element of continuity of personnel and them trying to justify themselves in this new context

themes.theme: War trauma, strategic loneliness and the turn to a deterrent

insights.claim: The Iran-Iraq war left the Islamic Republic in a condition of strategic loneliness and isolation that persists to this day, and that condition — not ideology alone — is why Iran built the Axis of Resistance.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: If proxies are a substitute for alliances rather than an ideological luxury, degrading them raises rather than lowers Iran's incentive to acquire a nuclear weapon.
insights.quote: strategic uh loneliness and isolation which to some extent persists to this day

insights.claim: Arms sales to Iran during the 1980s war were a lifeline for Chinese military industries, which were facing domestic austerity and had been forced to find their own customers to justify their existence.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A reminder that defense-industrial base survival often depends on sanctioned-buyer demand — relevant to reading today's Chinese and Russian export incentives.
insights.quote: they're now forced to go and kind of find their own customers to justify their existence

insights.claim: Israel was a supporter of Iran during the Iran-Iraq war, coordinating weapons and spare parts with the US, and there are implications Iran conducted a large-scale diversionary attack that widened the window for Israel's strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Iran-Israel hostility is a contingent post-1980s development, not a permanent structural fact — which keeps a low-probability realignment scenario alive.

insights.claim: Nuclear weapons entered the end-of-war politics as a rhetorical device: IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei's letter listing what was needed to continue the war — hundreds of thousands of troops, thousands of tanks, and nuclear weapons — was deliberately so unrealistic that it let the leadership justify accepting the ceasefire.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Iranian nuclear rhetoric has a long history of serving internal bureaucratic bargaining rather than signalling actual intent — a caution against reading every Tehran statement as strategy.
insights.quote: we need hundreds of thousands of more troops, we need like thousands of more tanks, oh, we need nuclear weapons

insights.claim: After the war the program de-internationalized sharply — Germany refused to complete Bushehr, Iran's Eurodif and Sofidif shares yielded no access to low-enriched uranium, and even an IAEA-brokered fuel supply effort in the 1980s failed — and that failure to meet civilian needs through cooperation is itself part of why the weapons option moved to the front.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Fuel-supply denial pushed Iran toward indigenous enrichment — the core argument against denying threshold states assured fuel access.

themes.theme: Rebuilding the weapons option: Amad, A.Q. Khan and the 2003 restructuring

insights.claim: US nonproliferation diplomacy in the 1990s successfully blocked Iranian nuclear cooperation with China, Argentina and others, leaving only Russia's completion of Bushehr — which Sabet calls probably one of Washington's greatest nonproliferation successes.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Supplier-side denial demonstrably works on the civilian track; it is the covert procurement track where it fails, which is where enforcement attention and sanctions risk concentrate.
insights.quote: the US has probably one of its greatest successes uh from a non-prololiferation perspective is is on the is on the nuclear side

insights.claim: Iran's wartime sanctions-evasion network of front companies, built to meet military needs, was repurposed to build the nuclear program's supply chain, alongside procurement from the A.Q. Khan Pakistani network.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Sanctions-evasion infrastructure is a durable, reusable capability — once built for one program it lowers the cost of every subsequent one, which is why sanctions relief rarely dismantles it.

insights.claim: The pre-2003 Amad program was concentrated, less compartmentalized and explicitly driven toward building a bomb, with the Shahab-3 developed partly as the delivery platform — a structurally different thing from the post-2003 effort.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Distinguishing the two eras matters for intelligence claims: evidence from the Amad archive does not automatically describe today's program structure.

insights.claim: A parallel Iranian Ministry of Defense effort to write a nuclear weapons doctrine reportedly ran counter to the weapons program itself, because former officials told Sabet the doctrinal implications for Iran's armed forces and security posture were unattractive — including becoming a target for existing nuclear weapons states.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Internal Iranian opposition to weaponization may come from the military itself on cost-benefit grounds, a channel outsiders rarely price into proliferation odds.
insights.quote: that doctrine effort to some extent ran counter to the weapons effort

insights.claim: After the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, Iran restructured the weapons option into three compartments: a main thrust on enrichment under civilian cover to master weapons-grade material, a missile program that could host a warhead, and a residual weaponization research effort inside a defense research institute analogous to DARPA.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The three-track structure explains why any deal limited to enrichment addresses only one leg — and why missile and weaponization files keep resurfacing as deal-breakers.

insights.claim: When the Islamic Republic justifies its large fuel cycle it recycles the Shah's topline numbers — 20,000 megawatts and the same plant plans — which functions as the civilian cover for the enrichment-first strategy.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A concrete tell for analysts: Iranian civil-nuclear demand claims are not built from current grid planning, so they should not be taken as evidence of genuine reactor procurement demand.
insights.quote: actually kind of regurgitating some of the Shaw's plans and the Shaw's topline ambitions

insights.claim: Iranian missiles have failure rates in the 10 to 20 percent range depending on type and production line, versus roughly 1 to 5 percent for a credible nuclear delivery platform, and warheads also need re-entry-hardened designs — so the missile force is not yet a usable nuclear delivery system.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A quantitative reason Iranian breakout timelines understate the real path to a deliverable weapon — and why Israeli sabotage of missile supply chains is strategically weighted.
insights.quote: 10% for a nuclear for a platform for nuclear weapons doesn't quite cut it

themes.theme: The sanctions bill: measuring what the program cost

insights.claim: Sabet and two MIT political science colleagues used synthetic control methodology — building a statistical counterfactual Iran from unsanctioned comparator countries — to price the macroeconomic cost of nuclear sanctions from 2010 to 2020.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A replicable method for quantifying sanctions damage in any sanctioned economy — useful for sizing the upside of relief scenarios in Iranian or Russian asset pricing.
insights.quote: the method basically builds a synthetic uh Iran statistically by mixing in other countries that don't have sanctions on them

insights.claim: The study found the economic cost of the nuclear sanctions Iran endured from roughly 2010 was equivalent to the economic cost of the Iran-Iraq war.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Sets the magnitude of what sanctions relief would be worth to Tehran — and therefore how much Iran should rationally concede to get it.
insights.quote: it was equivalent to the economic cost of the Iran war

insights.claim: The monetary figure Sabet recalls was not quite a trillion dollars but in the hundreds of billions, with the bulk attributable to nuclear sanctions rather than the counterterrorism, missile or human rights sanctions layered alongside them.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Quantifies the recoverable prize in a relief scenario, and identifies the nuclear file as the specific lever that controls most of it.
insights.quote: it wasn't quite a trillion but it was in the

insights.claim: After that spending and sacrifice, Iran has neither meaningful nuclear energy nor a nuclear deterrent to show for it — the central sunk-cost verdict of the episode.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: The negative return is itself a destabilizing input: a state that has already paid the full price of a weapon without owning one has weak incentives to stop short now.
insights.quote: And the country has neither meaningful nuclear energy or a nuclear deterrent to show for it.

themes.theme: JCPOA: systemic consensus, structural fragility, and Trump

insights.claim: Framing the JCPOA as a product of reformists winning power is an oversimplification: the nuclear program has been subject to consensus within the Iranian system since 2003, and factional identity affected only margins and execution quality.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Iranian elections are a weak signal for nuclear-deal odds; watch systemic consensus and IRGC posture instead when trading headline-driven Iran risk.
insights.quote: the subject to consensus within the system

insights.claim: The Oman back-channel talks began in mid-to-late 2012, well before the Iranian presidential election, with much of the groundwork laid under Ahmadinejad's government — evidence the shift was regime-level, not the arrival of a moderate president.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Back-channel initiation dates are the real leading indicator of a deal; presidential rhetoric lags them by a year or more.
insights.quote: the back channel Oman talks that secretary mentions those begin already mid to late uh 2013 sorry 2012

insights.claim: Sabet's published view is that the dominant and veto actor within the Islamic Republic, especially under the now-deceased supreme leader, has been the IRGC — meaning the JCPOA happened only because the Guards permitted it.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Any future deal is priced off IRGC acquiescence, not diplomatic teams — and the Guards' post-decapitation cohesion is now the key unknown.
insights.quote: especially during the rule of uh now deceased uh supreme leader has been the Islamic revolution guard court

insights.claim: The door to permitting some level of Iranian enrichment actually opened during the second term of the Bush administration, not under Obama, according to Sabet's post-doctoral sanctions research.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: US red lines on enrichment have moved before under a hawkish Republican administration — a precedent for a Trump-era accommodation that most models exclude.

insights.claim: Sabet judged the JCPOA's architecture logically strong but more vulnerable than most observers believed, because it resolved the strategic nuclear issue the P5+1 cared about while leaving the missile, drone and proxy issues that regional US allies faced day to day entirely unaddressed.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The same design flaw would afflict any narrow nuclear-only deal today — a reason to discount the durability of headline agreements that omit missiles and proxies.
insights.quote: the goal of the JCPOA and its architecture um had a had a strong logic to it, it was more vulnerable that I think more people believed

insights.claim: Iran's disappointing 2016-2017 sanctions relief was driven substantially by its own domestic conditions rather than residual sanctions: multinational country heads told Sabet they blamed sanctions in meetings with Iranian officials but privately cited protectionism by industry associations and currency market instability.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Sanctions relief alone would not unlock Iranian FDI — a caution against over-modelling the investment upside of any future deal without domestic reform.
insights.quote: our problem is like protectionism by this industry association or the instability in currency markets

insights.claim: Around the time the JCPOA was signed, Soleimani went to Moscow to organize the joint intervention in Syria and Iran surged support to the Houthis after their 2014 Sanaa coup — so Iranian regional escalation ran concurrently with the deal, hardening Israeli and GCC opposition.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Explains why nuclear diplomacy and regional escalation are not substitutes in Tehran's calculus — deals do not buy regional de-escalation.

insights.claim: Sabet argues Trump is personally a genuine Iran hawk as an ideological pillar rooted in 1979 and the hostage crisis — not merely captured by advisers like Pompeo or Bolton — but that this same standing makes him one of the few US presidents who could execute a Nixon-to-China comprehensive accommodation with the Islamic Republic.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Creates genuine two-sided tail risk on Iran headlines under Trump — both maximal escalation and a transformational deal are live, which argues for optionality rather than directional positioning.
insights.quote: actually Trump himself is a Iran hawk and I think he's shown that

themes.theme: Deterrence collapse and the Hormuz endgame

insights.claim: Iran's deterrence formula had roughly three and a half pillars — the Axis of Resistance proxy network, the missile and drone programs, and about half a pillar of advanced nuclear latency — plus air defense on the defensive side, and all have now been severely degraded or destroyed to varying degrees.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A pillar-by-pillar scorecard for judging Iranian escalation capacity — and the framework says the remaining capacity is concentrated in missiles and drones.
insights.quote: the act of resistance proxy network, the missile program and increasingly drone program

insights.claim: The missile and drone programs are the most intact and robust elements of Iranian power and the most likely to persist, ranking above the proxies.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Missile and drone risk to Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping stays elevated even as proxy risk fades — the relevant tail for insurance and regional asset pricing.
insights.quote: The missile program is the one that remain and the drone programs are the one that are the most intact, the most robust and likely to persist.

insights.claim: The proxy network is substantially broken: Assad's regime collapsed so the Syrian front never materialized, Hezbollah and the Iraqi Shia militias are significantly weakened and under disarmament pressure, and Hamas is degraded to a potential guerrilla actor rather than a rebuildable proxy force.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Removes the horizontal-escalation channel that historically capped Israeli and US action against Iran, raising the odds of direct state-on-state conflict.
insights.quote: Hezbollah is significantly weakened. The Iraq Shia militias are significantly weakened and under pressure there.

insights.claim: The Houthis are Iran's most robust remaining partner yet stayed largely out of the current conflict, launching only about two missiles at Israel, because they have taken enough economic and military damage to prefer retaining flexibility.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Red Sea shipping risk from Houthi action is currently self-limited by their own damage — a downward revision to freight and insurance risk premia unless the conflict widens.
insights.quote: they at one point they launched two missiles against Israel but that was kind of it

insights.claim: Iranian air defense has effectively failed: the US can obtain air superiority over Iran where and when it wants, demonstrated by the decapitation of dozens of first-tier and hundreds of second- and third-tier leadership figures across Iran's security sector.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: With no air-denial capability, Iran cannot protect fixed nuclear or energy infrastructure — meaning any Iranian reconstitution attempt is interdictable and escalation is cheap for the US.
insights.quote: decapitating dozens of what I would consider first tier leadership figures and hundreds of second and third tier uh leadership across Iran's uh security sector

insights.claim: Pre-war estimates that Iran could build and test one or two weapons within three to six months have been set back by the strikes, but the more important point is that one or two weapons do not constitute a deterrent.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Breakout-timeline headlines are the wrong metric; the tradeable question is time to a survivable arsenal, which is far longer.
insights.quote: conduct a nuclear test for one or two weapons you know within like 3 to 6 months that timeline has been set back

insights.claim: A small Iranian arsenal is more dangerous than none because it invites either a large-scale conventional attack or a nuclear strike, and given Israel's doctrine of not being the first to introduce nuclear weapons to the region, Sabet would not rule out at least a limited Israeli nuclear strike if Iran tested a weapon.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: The most severe tail scenario in the region is triggered by an Iranian test, not by Iranian enrichment — which is the event risk to hedge.
insights.quote: one or two weapons don't make a nuclear uh nuclear deterrent

insights.claim: Credible estimates put a robust Iranian deterrent — serialized warhead production plus delivery and possibly second-strike capability — at a minimum of two years even before the recent strikes, and that timeline must now be pushed out further.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Two-plus years is the real window for diplomacy or further military action — longer than the market's fixation on months-long breakout implies.
insights.quote: up to two years for serialized production of warheads

insights.claim: Sabet knows of no case of a country successfully executing a nuclear breakout or sneak-out, and notes Iran is deeply penetrated by hostile intelligence while its conventional deterrence is broken — making a dash for a weapon extremely dangerous even as it becomes politically more attractive inside Iran.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing near-term Iranian weaponization as likely, while flagging that domestic Iranian pressure for it is rising — a widening gap between intent and feasibility.
insights.quote: Iran's very penetrated from an intelligence perspective

insights.claim: Iran's public debate on nuclear weapons is active on domestic media despite suppression, but Sabet judges the pro-weapons side to be very uninformed about what operationalizing an arsenal actually requires.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Domestic pressure for weaponization is being built on faulty assumptions, which raises the risk of a strategically irrational Iranian decision.
insights.quote: if you watch the debate shows, this is one of the topics that it's often discussed

insights.claim: Closing the Strait of Hormuz and holding GCC critical energy infrastructure hostage partially restored Iranian deterrence during the last war, but its value is limited: Iran's declarations that the strait was closed were ignored by ships, control slipped away after the ceasefire, and it had to effectively restart a war to reimpose control.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: Empirically, Hormuz closure headlines overstate actual chokepoint control — a reason to fade oil spikes driven by declaratory closure without physical enforcement.
insights.quote: made statements that the straight is closed ships didn't listen to it

insights.claim: Sabet forecasts from private consulting work that between now and the end of this decade the share of crude, gas and derivatives passing through the Strait of Hormuz will drop dramatically from the roughly 15 to 20 percent level, and the region's overall importance will decline as petroleum investment shifts elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: A structurally declining geopolitical risk premium on Middle East energy through 2030 — bearish for the persistence of Hormuz-driven oil volatility and for Gulf strategic leverage.
insights.quote: the overall importance of the region will also decline as a percentage

insights.claim: Sabet's core trade thesis on Iran is that Hormuz was the real nuclear option and should have been traded in negotiations to end the conflict, because the card's value decays over time while the cost of playing it rises as GCC states build defensive, offensive and coalitional capacity.
insights.speaker: Farzan Sabet
insights.so_what: If Iran's best leverage is a wasting asset, the pressure to substitute with nuclear weapons rises through the late 2020s — the key mechanism linking energy geopolitics to proliferation risk.
insights.quote: the smart play in my view and this is something I've written about would have been then to trade that card
